activities.anchor: gut wall and liver enzymes attack it on the way through
activities.caption: rebuild a swallowed tablet's journey
activities.name: pbAdmeOrder

config.prompt: ADME, stage by stage — drag the journey into order:
items: Absorption: dissolve, survive stomach acid, cross the gut wall
First-pass metabolism: gut wall and hepatic enzymes take their toll en route
Distribution: blood flow, fat solubility and plasma protein binding decide where it travels
Metabolism: cytochrome P450 edits a lipid-soluble drug into a water-soluble one
Excretion: chiefly renal — failing kidneys raise levels the way failing livers do
config.why: Only the free, unbound fraction acts — a drug clipped to albumin is pharmacologically inert cargo, and competitors for the same albumin sites can suddenly unbind each other.

activities.anchor: Bioavailability is the whole point of the distinction
activities.caption: convert the route before the dose chart does
activities.name: pbMorphineEstimate

config.prompt: Oral morphine's bioavailability is around 30%. An intravenous dose is 10 mg. Roughly what oral dose delivers the same systemic amount?
config.why: 30% of 30 mg ≈ 10 mg — oral doses run roughly three times IV doses. Glyceryl trinitrate is the extreme case: almost completely destroyed by the liver, so it is given under the tongue into veins that bypass it entirely.

activities.anchor: is being told the truth of pharmacokinetics
activities.caption: set the five-half-life clock on the timeline
activities.name: pbSteadyPlace

config.prompt: A drug with a six-hour half-life is taken every twelve hours. Place the time to steady state:
config.why: About five half-lives — roughly thirty hours here — whatever the dose or interval. Halving the dosing interval narrows the peak-to-trough swing when a narrow window demands it; a loading dose fills the tank when waiting is intolerable.

activities.anchor: The clinical rule is the opposite
activities.caption: bet the doubled-dose outcome before the reveal
activities.name: pbMissedPredict

config.q: A patient on a wide-window antibiotic misses a dose and doubles the next. A patient on warfarin does the same. What distinguishes the two outcomes?
choices: The wide-window drug absorbs the extra peak; the narrow-window drug's peak pushes directly toward toxicity.
Doubling always restores the level that was lost.
Doubling halves the time to steady state in both cases.
config.why: Kinetics does not work in arrears: the extra dose adds a new peak on top of the current trough rather than restoring the lost level. Window width decides whether that peak is forgivable.

activities.anchor: Drug design is disproportionately the craft of widening the gap
activities.caption: pair each pharmacodynamic term with its reading
activities.name: pbReceptorMatch

config.prompt: Drugs act by binding — pair each term with its meaning:

pairs.right: binds and activates — adrenaline at beta-receptors speeds the heart
binds and blocks, denying the site to the body's own signal — beta-blockers quiet the same receptor
where the curve sits on the dose axis — decides the milligram count on the label
the height of the plateau — decides whether the drug can do the job at all

config.why: Selectivity is the third property: most "side effects" are the same key fitting other locks — H1 receptors in the brain drowse you, beta-2 receptors lining the airways constrict.

activities.anchor: Because of the plateau, doses above
activities.caption: one line of the dosing note misreads the ceiling
activities.name: pbPlateauSpot

config.prompt: A dosing note — one line confuses the curve's ceiling. Click it:
lines: The dose–response curve is a sigmoid: threshold, steep middle, plateau.
Potency is where the curve sits on the dose axis; efficacy is the plateau's height.
Above the plateau, higher doses add toxicity without adding effect.
So doubling a near-maximal dose roughly doubles the therapeutic effect as well.
For the patient, efficacy and toxicity are what matter; potency sets the milligram count.
config.correction: Doubling a near-maximal dose doubles nothing but the side effects — effect has a ceiling, toxicity does not.
config.why: The plateau is the whole point: past it, the only curve still rising is the toxicity curve.

activities.anchor: shows up first in the narrow-window drugs
activities.caption: file each drug by how much dosing slack it allows
activities.name: pbWindowBuckets

config.prompt: Two kinds of drugs in the pharmacopoeia — file each:

items.label: a missed or doubled dose rarely matters
warfarin — titrated to the individual, monitored by INR
digoxin, phenytoin, insulin — effective and toxic concentrations nearly touching

config.why: Therapeutic index = TD₅₀ / ED₅₀: above ~10 comfortable, under ~2 dangerous. A new antibiotic, NSAIDs or dehydration can destabilise a patient stable for years on warfarin — the narrow window is where shifts show first.

activities.anchor: transplant rejection on a herbal supplement
activities.caption: call the battleground enzyme's caseload
activities.name: pbCypEstimate

config.prompt: The cytochrome P450 family is where pharmacokinetic interactions fight. CYP3A4 alone handles roughly what share of all prescription drugs?
config.why: About half — which is why grapefruit juice's furanocoumarins, irreversibly disabling intestinal CYP3A4 for a day or more, can multiply a statin's blood level several-fold with no change in dose.
config.context: Inducers run the other way: rifampicin and St John's wort rev up CYP enzymes and can drop another drug below its window.
